The Inquisitor poses this problem: why do people not want to think for themselves? The answer lies in the soul's eternity and giving people time. He believes that after a million years, people will learn on their own that slavery is not what they want. God is forever patient; what matters is that people learn for themselves.

In Dante's Divine Comedy, the inquisitor asks why Jesus had to die. The Catholic Church teaches that when we do evil, we become slaves of Satan, and Jesus made a deal with him to free us. However, according to Dante, this doesn't make sense because if God freed us, He wouldn't want us to be slaves again. Instead, God came to free us so we could truly be free.

This is the power of forgiveness—showing love to even the most evil person can still spark change. The inquisitor's kiss on the prisoner symbolizes his loss and humility. Jesus' forgiveness does not change the old man's mind but leaves a spark that glows, representing the potential for redemption.

The Catholic Church and Jesus are competing forces; Dante challenges this teaching by questioning why Jesus had to die. According to the ransom theory, Jesus died so we could stop being slaves of Satan. However, Dante argues that God came to free us, not enslave us further.
